_note: Fictional sources for teaching: every source cited here is invented. See sources.json.
title: Making the sources talk to each other
context: A nursing student wants to argue for a change to how clinical placements are organised. They have notes on four sources.
question: Decide what each source can do for this claim.
claim: Clinical placements should build protected rest into nursing students' shifts.

summaries.text: Students on rotating shift patterns slept on average 1.4 hours less per night than students on fixed day shifts.

feedback.supports: Yes. This establishes the problem the claim responds to: shift patterns cost students sleep.
feedback.complicates: It doesn't push against the claim — it's the starting point for it. Shift patterns cost students sleep, which is the problem protected rest would address.
feedback.irrelevant: It's very relevant: it establishes the problem the claim responds to.

summaries.text: Poor sleep was associated with higher stress and lower placement assessment scores. The study could not show that poor sleep caused the lower scores.

feedback.supports: Yes — it explains why lost sleep matters. But keep its limit in mind: it shows an association, not a cause. A careful writer says so.
feedback.complicates: You've spotted something important: the study can't show cause. That's a limit to acknowledge, but overall the source still supports the claim by linking sleep to stress and performance.
feedback.irrelevant: It's relevant: it explains why lost sleep matters for students' learning.

summaries.text: On wards that introduced a scheduled 20-minute rest break, students reported less fatigue. However, the breaks were often skipped when wards were short-staffed.

feedback.supports: Partly — breaks did reduce fatigue. But the second finding complicates things: breaks only work if they actually happen. That is the most useful part of this source.
feedback.complicates: Yes. It supports breaks in principle, but shows they get skipped under pressure — which lets the writer sharpen the claim: rest has to be protected, not just offered.
feedback.irrelevant: It's directly relevant: it's the only source that tests rest breaks themselves.

summaries.text: Most nursing students said they would prefer placements in community settings rather than on hospital wards.

feedback.supports: It's about where students want to train, not about rest or sleep. Using it here would pull the paragraph off its point.
feedback.complicates: It doesn't really push against the claim — it's about a different question (where students want to train).
feedback.irrelevant: Yes. It's an interesting finding, but not for this claim. Leaving a source out is part of synthesis too.

synthesis: [[s1:Clinical placements should build protected rest into nursing students' shifts.]] [[s2:Students on rotating shifts sleep considerably less than those on fixed day patterns {{cite:lin2018}}, and poor sleep has been linked to higher stress and weaker placement performance {{cite:okafor2021}}.]] [[s3:The second finding is an association rather than proof of cause, but taken together the two studies suggest a plausible chain from shift pattern to sleep to performance.]] [[s4:Scheduled breaks appear to help: on wards where they were introduced, students reported feeling less tired {{cite:varga2023}}. The same study, however, found that breaks were often skipped when wards were short-staffed, which suggests that rest must be protected in the rota itself rather than left to the goodwill of busy teams.]]

annotations.s1: The paragraph opens with the writer's claim, not with a source.
annotations.s2: Two sources are linked in one sentence, each doing a different job: one shows the problem, the other shows why it matters.
annotations.s3: The writer evaluates the evidence (association, not cause) and says what the sources show together. This is the synthesis.
annotations.s4: The complicating source is used to sharpen the claim — 'protected' rest — rather than ignored. The fourth source has been left out.

notes.text: In numeric styles, the reader can't see who wrote what from the numbers alone. In a synthesis that doesn't matter much when you are combining findings — but when you weigh one source against another, consider naming the authors.

chefsNote: Synthesis shows how sources relate to each other, not just what each one says.
